notes:
Let me read the full Enduring Word page and a few verse-level commentary pages.I've put together notes for every verse except v. 35. I ran out of search and fetch requests before I finished, so some parts are thin:

- **Enduring Word:** the page cut off partway through vv. 26–27. I only saw its later sections through search snippets.
- **Sources I didn't reach:** the Wesleyan, Pentecostal (apart from Guzik), Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox and modern-scholarship sites, including NET notes and Bible Odyssey.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on this passage from prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teachers.

Those categories are missing below because I didn't find them, not because I checked and they had nothing to say.

**v. 24**
- Guzik says Solomon was eager to see justice done on Adonijah because he knew God had given him the throne. Solomon was zealous to give justice to Adonijah because he knew that God gave him the throne of Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/
- Guzik also says Solomon was only enforcing the "terms of parole" he set in 1 Kings 1:52. Solomon simply acted according to the "terms of parole" granted to Adonijah in 1 Kings 1:52… Adonijah made a wicked, treasonous request and is executed because of it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB, Presbyterian) says that, by the customs of the region, the request was a crime whether or not there was a hidden plot, and that Solomon can't be blamed for cruelty or for acting too hastily. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ki/1Ki_002.cfm
- Ligonier (Reformed) explains that in the ancient Near East, taking a ruler's concubine was a claim to his throne. As long as Adonijah lived, he was a threat to the kingdom, so Solomon removed him. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/adonijahs-treachery

**v. 25**
- Constable writes that Solomon correctly regarded Adonijah's request as an act of treason worthy of death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-25.html
- Precept Austin notes that Solomon sent Benaiah, one of their father's mighty men, to carry out the execution. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-2-commentary
- **A different view (bible.org):** this writer asks whether Bathsheba may have known what the request meant, so as to give Solomon an excuse to get rid of Adonijah? In any event, Solomon read an evil intent into the request. https://bible.org/series/%20http:/%7B%7D.?page=2177

**v. 26**
- Guzik says Abiathar deserved death because backing Adonijah went against both God's will and David's (1 Kings 1:7). This was treason against both God and the King of Israel. His comments on why Solomon spared him were cut off. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/
- Constable describes Solomon as giving Abiathar a parole for participating in Adonijah's rebellion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-27.html

**v. 27**
- Clarke: Abiathar was removed for siding with Adonijah, but this also fulfilled the prophecy of 1 Samuel 2. Abiathar was the last of the descendants of Ithamar, of which family was Eli the high priest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-27.html
- Gill (Baptist): the priesthood passed from Ithamar's line to Eleazar's, as foretold in 1 Samuel 2:31. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-27.html
- A commentator quoted on Bible Hub (citing Bähr) says another prophecy, about the priesthood belonging to Eleazar's line, came true here as well, and that no one can justly accuse Solomon of unnecessary severity or of cruelty toward Abiathar. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/2-27.htm
- Bible Hub's teaching notes say the verse shows that God's word comes to pass whatever people do. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/2-27.htm

**v. 28**
- The Pulpit Commentary says Joab's flight is almost certain evidence of his guilt, since Solomon had been generous before and Joab wouldn't have known David's last instructions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/2-28.htm
- JFB says Joab would have been executed long before if he hadn't been too powerful and popular with the army for the aging David to act. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-28.html
- Matthew Poole: people had begun treating the altar as a place of refuge by custom, not by any divine law, and Joab's case shows that refuge didn't cover murder. Poole also notes the tabernacle was then at Gibeon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/2-28.htm
- Bible Hub's notes read the "not with Absalom" line as showing Joab was pragmatic, not principled. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/2-28.htm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist), quoted by Guzik:** Joab ran to an altar he had rarely visited. Spurgeon applies this to people who hope to be saved by holding onto the altar *by sacrament*s. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

**v. 29**
- Matthew Henry: Solomon knew the law that the altar gave no protection to deliberate murderers (Exodus 21:14). In case of such sins as the blood of beasts would atone for the altar was a refuge, but not in Joab's case. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-28.html
- Gill mentions that Josephus says the order was to behead Joab. Gill suggests it may first have meant only to seize him and bring him to trial, since the Targum reads "exercise your power over him." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/2-29.htm

**v. 30**
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary calls "I will die here" a challenge to the king, as if Solomon wouldn't dare kill him there. But Joab had placed himself outside the protection of the altar. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-28.html
- JFB says Joab may have hoped religious scruples would stop anyone shedding blood at the altar, and that Benaiah passed the decision back to Solomon, who let the law take its course (Deuteronomy 19:13). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/2-28.htm
- Henry adds that Joab may have hoped Solomon would look like a defiler of the holy place if he killed him there. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-28.html

**vv. 31–32**
- Henry: Solomon based the sentence on the murders of Abner and Amasa rather than on Joab's support for Adonijah. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_002.cfm
- Henry also suggests that, given Joab's long service, Solomon might otherwise have pardoned him and simply removed him from command. https://ccel.org/ccel/henry/mhc2/mhc2.iKi.iii.html

**v. 33**
- JFB says this refers back to the curse David publicly pronounced on Joab in 2 Samuel 3:28–29. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ki/1Ki_002.cfm
- Constable: By executing Joab, Solomon cleared the way for God to bless him and his throne. God would punish Joab's house but bless David's house. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-2.html

**v. 34**
- Keil & Delitzsch: Benaiah "went up" because the altar stood higher on Mount Zion than Solomon's palace. Joab was buried in a tomb at his house. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-28.html
- Henry contrasts Joab with believers: those who hold onto Christ by faith shall find in him a more powerful protection than Joab found at the horns of the altar. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-28.html

**v. 35**
- I found no commentary on this verse beyond restatements of the text.

**vv. 36–37**
- Ellicott calls the order a sensible guard against treason. Mentioning the Kidron shows it was meant to keep Shimei away from his home town, Bahurim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/2-36.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the Kidron marked the city's eastern boundary, and Bahurim lay east of Jerusalem toward the desert. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/2-36.htm
- Coffman: Jerusalem then covered less than thirty-five acres, so this was a heavy restriction for a man who had led a thousand followers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-36.html
- Constable: Solomon made Jerusalem Shimei's prison and kept him away from his fellow Benjamites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-2.html

**v. 38**
- Guzik: Shimei knew Solomon was being merciful, and he was grateful for the arrangement as well as agreeing to it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/
- Henry calls this a fair trial of his obedience. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-36.html

**vv. 39–40**
- Precept Austin: Gath was about 20–25 miles from Jerusalem. Shimei's choice may show a low view of Solomon's authority or a high view of ability to fool Solomon. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-2-commentary
- Henry suggests Shimei saddled his donkey himself to keep the trip quiet. He quotes Bishop Hall: in chasing his servants, Shimei "lost himself." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-46.html
- The Expositor's Bible: Shimei apparently meant no harm. He thought that because he hadn't crossed the Kidron, Solomon wouldn't hear of it or wouldn't mind. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-kings-2.html

**vv. 41–43**
- Precept Austin: Shimei had wronged both God and the king. Breaking an oath sworn by the LORD was a spiritual offence, not just a personal failure. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-2-commentary
- Guzik thinks it was mostly carelessness or forgetting, but it was criminal to neglect or forget a royal covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/
- Keil & Delitzsch: there was no excuse. Shimei could have told the king and asked him to get the slaves back. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-46.html

**v. 44**
- Precept Austin: cursing a ruler was a capital crime (Exodus 22:28), so Shimei's death was within the limits of the law. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-2-commentary
- JFB: Shimei was executed for perjury, made worse by his earlier treason against David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/2-36.htm
- Henry's Concise Commentary warns that the old malignity remains in the unconverted heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/2-36.htm

**v. 45**
- Benson: "before the Lord" means in the sight of the God who sees and rewards just actions, or under His watch and blessing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-46.html
- Henry applies the verse to Christ: however much the church's enemies rage, Christ's throne is established, and they cannot shake it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-36.html

**v. 46**
- Gill: with the usurper and the general dead, the high priest deposed and Shimei gone, Solomon sat securely on his throne. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-46.html
- JFB: *all* the leaders of the rival factions had been cut off. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-46.html
- Constable: the section shows what happens to those who oppose God, namely loss of position or death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-2.html

**Where interpreters really differ (vv. 28–34 and 36–46)**

The split I found isn't between denominations. It runs between older writers who defend Solomon and some writers, including a Reformed one, who are more critical.

- **Defending Solomon:** the Pulpit Commentary admits that Shimei's execution has, perhaps, on the whole given more offence than that of Joab or even Adonijah. It still concludes that justice, morality, duty to his father and religion all justified it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-46.html
- **Critical of Shimei's execution (Ellicott):** it is hard to doubt the order was partly meant as a trap. Ellicott's verdict: Legally the execution was justifiable, and it may have been politic; but it cannot stand examination on the ground of equity or generosity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/2-36.htm
- **Critical (Ligonier, Reformed):** calls these some of the most troubling events of David's and Solomon's reigns. Killing Joab conveniently removed a possible rival, and he was killed at the altar. neither David nor Solomon come out of this episode looking innocent… Even the best saints fall far short of the glory of God. On Shimei, Ligonier says David kept the letter of his promise but broke its spirit. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joab-and-shimei-eliminated
- **Critical (bible.org):** Solomon set a trap which the avaricious Shimei fell into. https://bible.org/series/%20http:/%7B%7D.?page=2177
- **A reading of the background text (Clarke):** Clarke argues that David's charge in 2:9 should be read as "bring *not* down his hoar head… with blood." That would mean David never ordered Shimei's death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-2.html
- **Overview (Coffman):** the older, more conservative scholars all judged David's instructions fully justified. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-9.html
